title: Taurine and Betaine, Alone and in Combination, Mitigate Lysis of Canine Erythrocytes in an In Vitro Model of Iron-Deficiency Anemia

sections.abstract:
Dog anemia can result in symptoms such as lethargy, reduced appetite, weight loss, and dull coat, and in severe cases, it can become life-threatening. Currently available nutritional supplements for addressing anemia in pets often suffer from low bioavailability and significant side effects. This study investigates the effects of taurine and betaine on the survival and functionality of canine erythrocytes in vitro under conditions of nutritional anemia induced by the iron chelator desferrioxamine (DFO). Our findings indicate that taurine and betaine significantly enhance erythrocyte resilience and functionality in this specific in vitro model of nutritional anemia. Notably, this research sheds light on potential strategies for reducing lysis of canine RBCs in an in vitro model of iron deficiency.

Keywords: Taurine, Betaine, Pets, Dog anemia, Nutritional supplements
sections.introduction:
With the improvement in living standards, pet dogs have become loyal companions in an increasing number of households. However, alongside the rising number of pets, health issues in pets have become increasingly prominent ( Chikazawa and Dunning, 2016 , Thiele et al., 2023 , Tolbert, Murphy, Gaylord and Witzel-Rollins, 2022 ). Among these, anemia in pet dogs has garnered significant attention. Anemia refers to a condition in which the number of red blood cells (RBCs) or hemoglobin concentration in the blood falls below normal levels ( Newhall, Oliver and Anaemia, 2020 ). In pet dogs, the causes of anemia are diverse, including malnutrition ( Stanley, Appleman, Schlag and Siegel, 2019 ), chronic diseases ( Ferreira et al., 2017 ), parasitic infections ( Schoeman, 2009 ), and adverse drug reactions ( Trepanier, 2004 ). Anemia can lead to symptoms such as lethargy, reduced appetite, weight loss, and dull fur, and in severe cases, it can even be life-threatening ( Beck et al., 2019 , Fernandez, Sharman and Seth, 2020 ). Currently, various nutritional supplements targeting anemia in pets are available on the market, with primary ingredients such as iron ( Stoffel et al., 2020 ), vitamin B12 ( Temova Rakusa, Roskar, Hickey and Geremia, 2022 ), and folic acid ( Gomes et al., 2022 ). However, the effectiveness of these supplements varies greatly, and some products suffer from issues such as poor bioavailability and significant side effects ( Miller et al., 2024 , Reynolds, 2016 ). Consequently, identifying new and more effective nutrients has become a key focus of research.

Taurine ( Rafiee, Garcia-Serrano and Duarte, 2022 , Singh et al., 2023 ) and betaine ( Ashtary-Larky et al., 2022 , Willingham, Ragland and Ormsbee, 2020 ), well-known dietary supplements, have been reported to exhibit potential benefits in various physiological processes ( Fig. 1 A-B). Taurine may help support erythrocyte volume/osmotic homeostasis and thereby normal morphology, scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and modulates antioxidant enzymes to reduce oxidative damage to RBCs membranes and hemoglobin ( Seneff and Kyriakopoulos, 2025 ), regulates ion (Ca²⁺, K⁺, Na⁺) flux to maintain membrane potential ( Nandhini and Anuradha, 2003 ), and participates in bile acid conjugation and nutrient metabolism ( Persaud et al., 2021 ). Betaine functions as a methyl donor via the methionine-homocysteine cycle, supporting S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) synthesis for DNA/protein methylation essential. It also acts as an osmoprotectant to stabilize cell structure under stress, reduces homocysteine levels to alleviate cell fragility ( Kempson, Vovor-Dassu and Day, 2013 ), and enhances mitochondrial function/energy metabolism ( Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, their specific impact on erythrocytes in the context of nutritional anemia is not fully understood. This study aims to elucidate the effects of taurine and betaine on the survival and functionality of dog erythrocytes in an in vitro model of nutritional anemia induced by DFO, thereby providing foundational insights into their potential therapeutic applications.

sections.methods:
All experimental protocols strictly adhered to the ethical standards for ARRIVE Guidelines for Reporting Animal Research. All these studies were evaluated and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Nourse Centre for Pet Nutrition. Healthy Chinese farm dogs ( Canis lupus familiaris ) recruited through the Nourse Centre for Pet Nutrition. The dogs were aged between 2 and 5 years, and a total of 5 dogs were enrolled. Dogs were clinically healthy, housed under standard kennel conditions at the Centre, fed a commercial complete diet with water ad libitum, and received routine veterinary care. No experimental interventions were performed on the animals other than a single blood draw for each experiment.

Whole blood was collected from healthy dogs and anticoagulated using agents such as ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) to prevent clotting. Red blood cells (RBCs) were separated by centrifugation (3600 × g, 4 °C, 10 minutes), and the plasma and buffy coat were discarded. The RBCs were washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove residual plasma proteins and anticoagulants ( Dagur and McCoy, 2015 ). The washed RBCs were resuspended in PBS and divided into two groups, and the final hematocrit (HCT) was adjusted to 40%. One group of RBCs was cultured in complete medium (Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium, DMEM) as a control. The other group was cultured in a nutrient-deficient medium, which prepared by adding an 10uM iron chelator desferrioxamine (DFO) to the complete medium. All groups were incubated at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂ for different durations according to the detection indicators.

The collected RBCs were seeded into a 96-well plate at a density of 20,000 cells per well and treated with taurine (100 mM), betaine (10 mM), or PBS for 48 hours. Subsequently, the number of intact RBCs was quantified using a cell counter to assess cell survival rates.

RBCs from different treatment groups were centrifuged (3600 × g, 4 °C, 10 minutes), and the supernatant was collected. Hemoglobin concentration in the supernatant was measured using a hemoglobin ELISA kit (Shanghai Langton Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) to evaluate the extent of RBCs lysis.

RBCs from different treatment groups were centrifuged (3000 rpm, 10 minutes), and the supernatants were collected. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity in the supernatants was measured using an LDH ELISA kit (Shanghai Langton Biotechnology, Shanghai, China), serving as a supplementary indicator of RBCs lysis.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software version 9 (GraphPad Software, CA, USA). Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA, two-way ANOVA, and t-tests for comparisons between two groups, with results expressed as mean ± Standard Error of the Mean (SEM). All experiments were conducted in triplicate, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.results:
Feed ingredients are rich in nutrients such as proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals, which play critical roles in pet health ( Flickinger and Fahey, 2002 , Galli et al., 2024 ). Initially, we conducted a literature review to screen common feed ingredients available in the market and identified three candidate substances: taurine, betaine, and cellulase. Dog RBCs were treated with taurine (100 mM), betaine (10 mM), and cellulase (1%) for various durations, and hemoglobin concentration were assessed using an ‌ELISA assay. The results showed that taurine and betaine treatment enhanced hemoglobin concentration in dog RBCs ( Fig. 1 C-D; Table 1 , Table 2 ), while cellulase had no effect. These findings suggest that taurine and betaine have the potential to improve anemia in an in vitro model, prompting their selection for further studies and validation.

During dog anemia, RBCs often exhibit irregular or deformed shapes, accompanied by significantly reduced viability. Deferoxamine (DFO) potentially induces hemolysis or oxidative membrane damage in erythrocytes via chelation of labile iron pools and perturbation of redox homeostasis, and was therefore employed to simulate a nutritional anemia environment in the present study. We added the iron chelator DFO to the dog RBCs culture medium and subsequently treated the cells with taurine and betaine. The results demonstrated that RBCs viability was markedly impaired under nutrient-deficient conditions. However, treatment with taurine or betaine restored RBCs survival rates to normal levels ( Fig. 2 A-B; Table 3 , Table 4 ), indicating that these nutrients can enhance RBCs viability under conditions of nutritional anemia.

Anemia in dogs leads to a reduction in hemoglobin content within RBCs, rendering them fragile and prone to rupture. Consequently, hemoglobin and LDH are released from RBCs into the culture medium. To investigate this, we treated dog RBCs with taurine and betaine and measured the concentrations of hemoglobin and LDH in the culture supernatant. The results showed that in the group treated with DFO alone, hemoglobin levels in the supernatant were significantly higher compared to the control group. This effect was notably reversed by treatment with taurine and betaine ( Fig. 3 A-B; Table 5 , Table 6 ). Similarly, LDH levels were significantly elevated in the DFO-treated group compared to the control group, and this increase was also effectively mitigated by taurine and betaine ( Fig. 3 C). These findings demonstrate that these nutrients can reduce the rupture of dog RBCs.

In some cases, a single nutrient may not fully control a disease or symptom, or may require higher doses to achieve the desired effect, potentially increasing the risk of adverse reactions. The combined use of nutrients can achieve better therapeutic outcomes at lower doses while reducing the incidence of side effects. The results above demonstrate that taurine and betaine independently reduce hemolysis in dog RBCs. This prompted us to investigate whether the combined treatment with these two nutrients would yield synergistic effects. Following DFO treatment, groups treated with taurine or betaine alone exhibited similar trends in hemoglobin and LDH release as previously observed. Notably, when taurine and betaine were used in combination, the release of hemoglobin and LDH was significantly reduced to levels comparable to the control group, indicating the strongest protective effect ( Fig. 4 A-B; Table 7 ).

sections.discussion:
The raw materials in pet feed contain a wide array of essential nutrients, including proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals, all of which play a critical role in the health of pets. By screening and investigating specific components within these feed ingredients, it is possible to identify nutrients that can effectively improve anemia in pets ( Swanson et al., 2013 ). This not only enhances the added value of the feed but also provides more comprehensive nutritional support for pets ( DeBeer et al., 2024 ). This project focuses on screening two nutrients: taurine and betaine, which from feed ingredients that demonstrate potential in improving anemia in pet dogs. Through cellular experiments, we evaluate the effectiveness of taurine and betaine in improving anemia in pet dogs, including their protective effects on the growth, vitality, and integrity of dog RBCs. The findings aim to provide a theoretical basis for the development of novel pet feed additives. The implementation of this research will contribute to addressing anemia in pet dogs and cats, enhancing their health and quality of life. Furthermore, the outcomes of this project could offer new research directions and product development strategies for the pet feed industry, thus promoting innovation and development within the pet feed market.

Taurine and betaine’s observed protective effects in our DFO-induced model may stem from various aspects, though direct validation in canine nutritional anemia is pending. For example, Taurine’s effects may relate to osmoprotection, membrane stabilization, and HOCl scavenging. Preclinical studies indicate taurine reduces erythrocyte osmotic hemolysis to preserve biconcave shape ( Gao et al., 2022 ), suppresses radical-induced hemolysis in canine erythrocytes via membrane interactions ( Nakamura et al., 1993 ), and forms less toxic taurine chloramines to mitigate oxidative damage ( Koyama et al., 1996 ), consistent with our data showing reduced LDH release and restored RBC survival. Betaine’s efficacy likely involves methyl donation and osmoprotection. As a methyl donor, it may replenish S-adenosylmethionine to support globin methylation and hemoglobin synthesis ( Craig, 2004 ), while its homocysteine-lowering effect could reduce erythrocyte fragility ( Peschen, 1999 ). It also stabilizes cell structure under stress via osmoprotective properties ( Lerche and Bilsing, 1988 ).

The findings of this study confirm the potential of taurine and betaine in improving the survival and functionality of dog erythrocytes under conditions of nutritional anemia. The supplementation of these compounds demonstrates promising results in enhancing RBCs resilience and preserving their critical functions, which is particularly significant in the management of nutritional anemia in dogs. The elucidation of the mechanisms underlying the effects of taurine and betaine on RBCs will provide valuable insights into the development of targeted nutritional strategies for addressing dog health concerns related to anemia.
